articles.title_orig: Apple earnings live updates: New CEO John Ternus faces first Wall Street test
articles.title_zh: Apple earnings live updates: New CEO John Ternus faces first Wall Street test
articles.content_orig:
Apple reports fiscal fourth-quarter earnings after the bell on Monday, with new CEO John Ternus expected to address Wall Street in a meaningful way for the first time.
Here's what analysts are expecting, according to LSEG.
Revenue is expected to increase 11% from $102.5 billion a year earlier. Analysts project $56.59 billion in iPhone sales for the quarter.
Wall Street is closely watching iPhone revenue because the report will include eight days of new iPhone 18 Pro sales. But Apple's new flagship device, the iPhone Duo, didn't hit store shelves until the quarter was over, and Apple didn't announce a new entry-level iPhone 18.
Apple also raised prices on iPhones by $100, which may have hurt demand in the quarter.
Monday's earnings call, set to start at 5 p.m. ET, will be the first with Ternus at the helm. Investors want to hear from him about the company's plans in China after its AI software got approved, as well as the slew of recent product launches and how the company continues to grapple with global shortages of memory and flash storage.
Monday is an unusual day for Apple to report earnings. The iPhone maker typically schedules earnings for Thursday, although it has mixed in Tuesdays and Wednesdays.
The last time the company reported earnings on a Monday was on April 27, 2015.
Apple spent the weekend as the most valuable publicly traded company, after taking the crown from Nvidia at market close on Friday.
But Apple shares slipped about 2% on Monday, and the two are neck and neck at around $4.91 trillion. The two companies have been swapping at the top of the table for years. Before this month, Apple passed Nvidia in July, but Nvidia quickly reclaimed the top spot a few days later.
While Monday's earnings report won't include sales from the iPhone Duo, execs may still be pressed on the device's launch in October.
There hasn't been much supply of the folding iPhone, with first-day preorders quickly slipping into estimated ship dates in 2027.
But there are also a number of reports that the Duo can crack under normal use, which is a tough hit to Apple's brand under Ternus. Apple acknowledged the issues last month and said they affected a "small number" of devices.
Analysts at Barclays wrote in an earnings preview over the weekend that they "remain cautious on the stock given iPhone uncertainties this cycle, limited monetization of AI, and renewed fears on the App Store."
The firm has an underweight rating on the shares, and said the "pricing benefits AAPL has been enjoying from the memory backdrop due to its scale and preferential pricing are fading."
Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan said on Friday that his team had a "conservative outlook" on earnings because of gross margin concerns and price increases.
The analyst pointed out that Apple's gross margins in the September quarter will be boosted by a positive impact from tariff refunds, and that margins could drop in the coming quarters.
Apple reported a gross margin of 49.3% in its June quarter, but warned that it would be between 47.5% and 48% in the September period.
"Investor focus will likely be on component cost inflation, durability of gross margin and services revenue growth," Mohan wrote in the note.
Bank of America maintains a Buy rating on the stock and a price target of $370.
Apple is competing in a smartphone and PC market that has "never been worse," IDC's Ryan Reith told CNBC.
Consumer electronics companies everywhere are grappling with surging prices for computer parts, including memory and flash storage that's used in every smartphone and laptop.
Intel on Friday had its worst day on the stock market since the 1970s, dropping 29%, after the company cited PC softness for a disappointing forecast .
Many companies have responded to component shortages by raising prices or reducing specifications for current devices. Consumers are holding onto their old computers for far longer, driving sales down.
IDC says the smartphone market is set to drop nearly 17% this year based on shipments. PCs could be down 11%.
Apple isn't immune. The company raised prices on almost all of its products since executives warned over the summer that the market was in a "thousand year flood."
Apple's new $2,000 foldable phone won't have any sales for the quarter, which ended last month. While Apple and Ternus announced new iPhones on Sept. 9, the foldable Duo didn't go on sale until a month later, on Oct 23.
Some analysts have theorized that Apple's most committed fans may have been waiting to see the Duo come out before buying it.
There will be a few weeks of sales from the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, which went on sale on Sept. 18.
Apple investors and customers are still getting to know Ternus, but since he took over for Tim Cook on Sept. 1, the new CEO has embraced his new role as the face of the iPhone company.
Ternus' first major appearance came nine days into his tenure, when he unveiled the iPhone Duo at Apple's headquarters. A week later, he was walking the red carpet at the Emmys. He then flew to New York, where he opened the doors at an Apple store to commemorate the new iPhone Pro going on sale. He also went to Austin, Texas, this month to kick off sales of the iPhone Duo, and appeared at an elementary school and an F1 race while on the trip.
And he's had a busy media schedule, including an appearance on the cover of Time magazine.
Last week, Ternus continued a new style of Apple product introduction in unveiling the first MacBook with a touchscreen using a format he first tried out in the spring. That's when Apple launched its low-cost MacBook Neo. Ternus addressed a crowd of media and analysts, giving a five minute speech interspersed with a few short videos.
Investors will get their first in-depth look at Ternus on Monday. He's been on the past few calls, but hasn't given extended remarks, and largely deferred to Cook when asked questions.
Heading into its earnings report, Apple has emerged as the preferred megacap tech stock on Wall Street. The shares are up 27% this year as of Friday's close, by far outpacing Apple's leading peers.
It's also the last among the group (other than Nvidia, which reports next month) to issue quarterly earnings. Investors weren't kind to the hyperscalers over the past two weeks, scrutinizing their hefty expenses and dwindling cash flows.
Apple is in a much different category as the iPhone maker has avoided running up huge capital expenditures bills, taking a more measured approach to its AI investing.

articles.title_orig: Oil Futures Slump As Iran Peace Efforts Ease Supply Fears
articles.title_zh: Oil Futures Slump As Iran Peace Efforts Ease Supply Fears
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signalled they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures shed 7.4% to close at $96.46 a barrel, the biggest daily loss since July 27. Brent crude , the international benchmark, lost 7.6% to settle at $104.77 a barrel.
President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that Iran wants to "make a deal and that could happen." U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend that Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections, gaining more than 10% in October.
The oil market has sold off during previous phases of the war on rumors of a possible settlement, only for the conflict to subsequently escalate and spike prices again.
Trump "hasn't made a decision" on whether to strike Iran again, Rubio told reporters.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency . Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government certain authorities to do this, Pezeshkian said.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to IRNA.
Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said.
But Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian and Russian emergency alert apps send false warnings after hacks
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian and Russian emergency alert apps send false warnings after hacks
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine's air force said Sunday its Air Alert app had been compromised after it reportedly sent false warnings of nuclear and chemical threats in Kyiv and other areas.
The app briefly displayed alerts for nuclear and chemical incidents as well as warnings of street fighting, according to Reuters. The air force said unauthorized persons had interfered with the app's operation and that it had temporarily disabled push notifications.
"There is no radiation threat! Stay calm, follow our messages on our channel," the air force said on Telegram, according to a translation.
Two hours later, Russia's Ministry for Emergency Situations said its mobile app had been subject to "a massive cyberattack, allowing attackers to send fake information to the public."
It was not immediately clear if the incidents were linked. CNBC has reached out to Russian and Ukrainian authorities for comment.
The alleged cyberattacks come as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on each other's territories and infrastructure.
Overnight, a local ceasefire in the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky and surrounding areas in the Kherson region, near the Crimean Peninsula, expired. The temporary pause in fighting allowed humanitarian aid to enter the city and the evacuation of hundreds of people who had been trapped largely without access to food, water, electricity and medicine.
It was the longest local ceasefire since the full-scale invasion began in early 2022, and both parties appeared to have honored the pause until it ended at midnight Moscow time.
On Monday morning, local media reported that Russian forces had struck a hospital in central Kherson, while Ukraine's General Staff of Armed Forces said Moscow had used the ceasefire to reinforce its military positions in the city.
"During the ceasefire, the rotation of Russian units, the fortification of positions, the expansion of anti-drone measures along roads and increased logistics activity, including the delivery of ammunition, were recorded," the military body said early Monday.
On Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said October had been the deadliest month for Russia since the invasion began in 2022.
Over the past month, Russia lost 54,400 troops killed or badly wounded, "a record for any month of the full-scale war," Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine's Defense Forces liberated 96.2 square kilometers (37.1 square miles) of Ukrainian land in October – 10.4 square kilometers more than Russia captured during that time.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran says "ball is in the U.S. court" on deal to end war as Trump keeps his intentions veiled
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran says "ball is in the U.S. court" on deal to end war as Trump keeps his intentions veiled
articles.content_orig:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has asked the Supreme Court to stop California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are not US citizens.
The emergency request, filed on Monday, just one day before the midterm elections , is the latest development in a legal battle between the administration and California, a Democratic stronghold and the most populous US state.
California says the move could disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters.
The Department of Justice wants the Supreme Court to step in immediately and force California to set aside ballots from voters on a list compiled by the Department of Homeland Security until after their citizenship status can be verified.
The department argues once the ballots are mixed in with others, there would be no way to identify them and remove them if the voters were later found to be ineligible.
But California says the list is unreliable and could include thousands of US citizens.
Voting has been under way since early October, with ballots mailed to around 23 million registered voters and hundreds of thousands already processed. State officials say it would be nearly impossible to separate the ballots in question.
Last week, a federal judge rejected the administration’s request, raising concerns about the reliability of the data on the list.
“If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” Judge David Carter wrote.
The administration has turned to the Supreme Court after a federal appeals court also rejected the request on Friday.
It is not clear when the Supreme Court, which rejected an earlier effort to restrict mail-in voting in September, will rule. The case will be handled by Justice Elena Kagan, who hasn’t set a deadline yet for California to respond.
The dispute comes as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress in Tuesday’s elections.
Trump has repeatedly made false claims about widespread voter fraud, but studies and state audits have shown that ineligible voting, including by noncitizens, is rare.

articles.title_orig: Poland's constitutional crisis deepens as Prime Minister Tusk faces accusations of power grab
articles.title_zh: Poland's constitutional crisis deepens as Prime Minister Tusk faces accusations of power grab
articles.content_orig:
Protesters gathered outside Poland’s top court as a long-running political dispute involving President Karol Nawrocki and Donald Tusk’s government escalated.  (AP Video.)
Friday’s late-night confrontation at Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, which drew riot police and protesters and prompted President Karol Nawrocki to turn his plane around and return to Warsaw, has reignited a bitter debate over whether Prime Minister Donald Tusk is restoring the rule of law or overstepping constitutional limits.
The dispute erupted after the tribunal announced the suspension of its president, Bogdan Święczkowski, a move that supporters of Tusk’s government described as necessary to restore judicial independence, while critics denounced it as an unconstitutional power grab.
Marcin Przydacz, the head of the International Policy Bureau in Nawrocki’s office, took to European TV Monday morning denouncing Tusk’s actions, saying, "Even lawyers who are close to the Tusk government say that there's absolutely no legal basis for such behavior."
POLISH PRESIDENT TURNS PLANE AROUND AFTER 'COUP' AT NATION’S TOP COURT
Donald Tusk, Poland's prime minister, during the Polish Army Parade in Warsaw on Aug. 15, 2025. (Damian Lemanski/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The dispute is also triggering diplomatic fallout, with at least three Polish ambassadors resigning in protest. Przydacz, a former parliament member of the now-opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, says Poland’s permanent representative to the U.N. since 2021, Krzysztof Szczerski, resigned Monday, which followed the resignations over the weekend of the ambassadors to China and Romania.
"This crisis didn’t begin on Friday," said Simone Rodan‑Benzaquen, senior envoy to Europe at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. "Poland has been living with a deeply compromised Constitutional Tribunal for more than a decade."
Rodan-Benzaquen said the confrontation cannot be understood in isolation. Parliament has continued appointing judges under Poland's constitution, but several of those appointments have been blocked from taking office amid a years-long standoff between the government, the presidency and the tribunal itself.
Presidential candidate Karol Nawrocki, a conservative historian backed by the right-wing Law and Justice party, second right, greets supporters at his headquarters after the presidential election runoff in Warsaw, Poland, June 1, 2025. (AP Photo/Czarek Sokolowski)
"This isn't simply a case of Tusk deciding to pack a functioning, independent court ahead of an election," Rodan-Benzaquen tells Fox News Digital. "There is a genuine institutional crisis that predates his government, and a legitimate question of how to resolve it."
That underlying conflict exploded into public view Friday after Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska suspended Święczkowski and his deputy, triggering protests outside the tribunal and prompting Nawrocki to abandon a trip to Senegal. Police detained three people after some demonstrators clashed with officers outside the court complex.
HUNGARY AND POLAND DEFEND TOUGH MIGRATION POLICIES AS FRANCE REELS FROM VIOLENT UNREST
Rodan-Benzaquen cautioned that concerns about Friday's actions are not limited to supporters of the opposition, saying they "raise serious questions about the legality and proportionality of the methods being used."
Critics of the government have described Friday's events as an unprecedented assault on Poland's constitutional order. "My former boss, Margaret Thatcher, would have been absolutely appalled by what we're witnessing in Poland," Nile Gardner, director of the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at the Heritage Foundation told Fox News Digital. "This is clearly a crisis for Poland and an attempted coup by Donald Tusk."
"This has all the hallmarks of a Soviet-style coup operation," added Gardner, who said Tusk waited until Nawrocki was traveling out of the country, accusing the prime minister of undermining the tribunal and further destabilizing Poland ahead of next year's election. "It's the sort of thing you'd expect actually from a third world dictator."
Protesters gather outside the headquarters of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw after police blocked access to the court building on Oct. 30, 2026 (Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images)
Others reject the coup characterization. Boštjan Udovič, chair of international relations at the University of Ljubljana, says the dispute centers on the government's attempt to restore judicial arrangements that critics of the previous PiS government say were inconsistent with both Poland's constitution and European legal standards.
"Tusk wants to restore the situation as required by the constitution and the international institutions," Udovič said. "I think that he hoped the transition would be easier."
Tusk defended his government's actions as part of an effort to restore the rule of law, accusing both the president and the tribunal of improperly blocking judges elected by parliament from taking office. "The solution to the conflict is simple," he said on Monday. "The president recognizes the judges legally elected by [parliament], because that is what the Constitution stipulates." He accused Nawrocki of "choosing forceful confrontation, which could cost Poland very dearly. A democratic state under the rule of law cannot yield to violence."
POLAND ARRESTS RUSSIAN ALLEGEDLY HIRED TO KILL UKRAINIAN-AMERICAN WHO WAS 'INCONVENIENT TO THE PUTIN REGIME'
"Restoring the rule of law is essential," Rodan-Benzaquen says, warning against viewing the dispute purely through a partisan lens. "But the legitimacy of that restoration depends not only on its objectives, but also on the legality of the means used to achieve it."
The divide in Poland has increasingly been reflected abroad, with European institutions and political leaders offering sharply different interpretations of the crisis.
Protesters rally outside Poland’s top court as tensions between President Karol Nawrocki and Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government intensify. (AP)
The European Commission has largely backed the Polish parliament's authority to appoint judges. European Commissioner Michael McGrath said selecting new judges lies within the powers of Poland's parliament.
French opposition leader Marine Le Pen , meanwhile, accused Brussels of applying a double standard. "One cannot claim to defend democracy and the rule of law while remaining silent when the constitutional balance of a member state is gravely threatened," she posted on X. "The proliferation of such strong-arm tactics within the European Union itself is beginning to raise serious questions."
"America is on Poland’s side," U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose posted to X , urging restraint. "Our concern is for the stability, security, and democratic future of a country we are proud to call our friend and ally… Poland has come too far and accomplished too much to let political differences, no matter how strongly felt, put any of that at risk."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Police were deployed outside the Constitutional Tribunal after Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, elected by the Parlament in March 2026, issued an order suspending Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski and Vice President Bartlomiej Sochanski from their duties for one month. (Kai Taller/Arena Akcji/Sipa USA)
For Rodan-Benzaquen, the larger issue extends far beyond the events of Friday night. "One side claims to be defending constitutional order against the abuses of the other, while the institutions that should arbitrate the dispute have themselves become the object of the dispute," she said.
With parliamentary elections in Poland only a year away, the battle over who gets to define the rule of law may prove more consequential than the confrontation that unfolded this weekend.

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: S&P 500, Nasdaq rebound sputters, Dow edges higher as oil prices fall
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: S&P 500, Nasdaq rebound sputters, Dow edges higher as oil prices fall
articles.content_orig:
Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington.
The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections.
A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022.
Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week.
"There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well."
Still, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress.
Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control.
"If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said.
Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year.
Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance.
The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff.
Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale.
Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election.
The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says.
But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment.
The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates.
"Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note.
If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge.
— CNBC's Chris Hayes contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: As peacekeepers leave Western Sahara, refugees yearn to end a half-century wait
articles.title_zh: As peacekeepers leave Western Sahara, refugees yearn to end a half-century wait
articles.content_orig:
The conflict pits Morocco, which considers the region its own, against the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, which seeks a separate state
At 51, Binina Mohamed is as old as the conflict that drove her from the Western Sahara region into a refugee camp in southern Algeria, where she has spent her life among tens of thousands of others facing a similar fate.
The confrontation over her native land, often described as Africa’s longest-running territorial dispute, was brought back into focus this weekend by a UN Security ‌Council row that led to the end of a decades-old peacekeeping mission there.
The Western Sahara conflict pits Morocco, which considers the territory its own, against the Algeria-backed Polisario Front, a political and military organisation that has been seeking a separate state there since the departure of former colonial power Spain in 1976. Peacekeepers have watched over the territory since 1991, when the UN brokered a ceasefire ending years of guerrilla warfare between the two sides.

articles.title_orig: New CB90 CX Is Bigger, Optionally Crewed Evolution Of Saab’s Proven Combat Boat
articles.title_zh: New CB90 CX Is Bigger, Optionally Crewed Evolution Of Saab’s Proven Combat Boat
articles.content_orig:
Saab is taking its well-established CB90 combat boat in a notably more ambitious direction, introducing a larger, optionally crewed version that’s intended to do much more than ferry troops and conduct raids. The new Combat Boat 90 Capability X (CB90 CX) is being developed as a multi-mission combat platform capable of carrying sensors and weapons for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), anti-surface warfare, and short-range air defense (SHORAD).
The new boat represents a significant evolution of a design that has been adopted by naval forces around the world for littoral operations. Compared to the original design, however, the CX adds greater payload capacity, updated onboard systems, and the ability to operate with or without a crew.
Saab says the CB90 CX is currently in production for Sweden, which will be the launch customer, with 36 craft under contract for the Swedish Amphibious Battalion . With the Swedish Armed Forces, the new boat will operate alongside the existing, smaller CB90 NG rather than immediately replacing it.
The development reflects several broader shifts in naval warfare, including the use of smaller combatants to contribute directly to the fight rather than simply transport personnel or support larger ships. At the same time, the ability of the CB90 CX to operate without personnel on board is indicative of the rapid advances being made in the uncrewed surface vessel (USV) space.
“The future of naval operations is not just about having more platforms; it is about distributing greater combat capability across the force,” Anders Hellman, head of Saab’s Docksta business unit, said in the announcement.
Hellman also pointed to recent operations in the Baltic Sea , the Black Sea, and the Red Sea to highlight the kinds of areas and missions the CB90 CX has been designed to face. In the Baltic, this includes protection of critical infrastructure as the threat from Russia continues to grow. In the Black Sea , Russia and Ukraine have been engaged in extensive naval warfare , increasingly using USVs to undertake missions including attacks on shipping and against ground targets, as well as SHORAD . Finally, the Red Sea has seen USVs, aerial drones, and cruise missiles attack commercial shipping , with the sheer volume of these strikes putting traditional naval air defenses under extreme pressure .
The baseline CB90 has already established its reputation through a combination of speed, maneuverability, and the ability to operate in confined coastal waters. While developed specifically with Swedish naval operations in mind, it has also been adopted by close to a dozen navies around the world. Among its operators, U.S. Navy examples are designated as the Riverine Command Boat . More unusually, Russia has fielded a locally developed clone of the CB90 design, known as the Raptor class .
The CB90 CX keeps those features but combines them with a larger hull and increased payload capacity, meaning it can accommodate a wider range of mission systems and weapons.
The ability for the CX to operate as an optionally crewed boat is derived from Saab’s proprietary Autonomous Ocean Core system. The company has not yet disclosed the full details of the autonomous operating modes but says that human supervision will be required as part of the decision-making process. Saab also says that every CB90 CX will come with the option of autonomous operations, with the decision falling upon the operator, based on the particular mission requirements.
Clearly, the combination of a larger platform and autonomous operation opens up a range of possibilities for employing the boat in situations where putting a crew at risk may be undesirable. The CX is also designed to operate across a wider range of sea states.
In terms of specifications, the CB90 CX has an overall length of 59 feet, compared to 54.5 feet for the CB90 NG variant. It is powered by a pair of 1,100-horsepower engines driving waterjets, giving a maximum speed of over 40 knots, at which it can travel for more than 300 nautical miles. In crewed configuration, it can carry up to 10 personnel.
The ISR variant is designed to provide enhanced situational awareness across multiple domains. It incorporates Saab’s Giraffe 1X X-band 3D surveillance radar, which can detect and track threats in the air and on the surface, out to a range of over 62 miles against aerial targets. The radar is mounted on a 36-foot extending mast to increase its range over the horizon and in littoral zones.
The anti-ship warfare configuration is intended to provide over-the-horizon strike capability against surface vessels. Saab has shown a rendering of this version armed with a pair of MBDA’s Marte ER anti-ship missiles in angled canisters.
Marte ER is a lightweight, long-range missile designed to be deployed from a wide range of platforms, including aircraft, coastal batteries, and smaller naval vessels. It has a range of over 62 miles and operates on a sea-skimming ‘fire-and-forget’ principle, guided by an active radar seeker. The missile can also be employed against land targets, a capability that Saab doesn’t explicitly mention.
However, Marte ER is just one option for the CB90 CX, and Saab has confirmed that Sweden will arm the boats with a different, undisclosed missile.
Furthermore, both the ISR and anti-ship versions are armed with a 12.7mm or 30mm Trackfire Remote Weapon Station for self-defense.
The SHORAD configuration, meanwhile, is designed to address the growing threat posed by drones. It will employ Rheinmetall’s Seasnake 30mm autocannon, giving the boat a dedicated close-range air defense role. As well as drones, the gun, which has a nominal maximum rate of fire of 1,100 rounds per minute, can be used to engage helicopters, and it has a secondary role against surface targets, including USVs.
The latter capability is particularly notable as navies increasingly face the challenge of defending themselves against relatively inexpensive drones that can threaten even sophisticated warships.
Beyond these three initial mission variants, Saab says it is developing an option to launch drones from the CB90 CX. Both tube-launched drones and quadcopters are being examined. Torpedo armament is also planned as an option.
The broader concept behind the CB90 CX involves the distribution of sensors and weapons across a larger number of smaller, more flexible platforms, which may or may not be crewed.
Operators could employ multiple CB90 CX boats in complementary roles. ISR-equipped boats could help detect and track threats, while anti-ship variants provide additional strike options, and SHORAD-equipped boats help protect the force against aerial threats.
Operating together, the different configurations could create a more distributed and more resilient combat fleet, particularly in coastal environments where geography, island chains, and confined waterways complicate operations.
Furthermore, the optionally crewed version would allow the boats to operate in higher-risk areas or undertake missions that would otherwise expose personnel to unacceptable danger.
The ISR variant, in particular, could be of use in a scenario like the current crisis with Iran, for instance. Vessels equipped with the Sea Giraffe radar could form a picket line across the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz, and Gulf of Oman to detect incoming drones and cruise missiles, and also provide data on surface movements. A counter-drone variants could be used for force protection. The idea that these could even be uncrewed makes such an application even more attractive considering the threats posed to vessels in this region and especially in or near the strait.
For Sweden, the introduction of the CX alongside the CB90 NG means that a more capable combat boat can be introduced alongside the smaller platform, which remains useful for more traditional troop transport and raiding party missions.

articles.title_orig: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
articles.title_zh: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
articles.content_orig:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has set out plans to overhaul immigration rules.
Proposals to change the requirements to qualify for permanent settlement in the UK were first outlined in detail in November 2025, when Mahmood was home secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government.
Following a consultation , Mahmood has now announced her final decision on what changes should be taken forward.
Indefinite leave to remain (ILR) – also known as settlement – gives someone the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like.
Under the current system, people with ILR can also apply for benefits if they are eligible.
People who have lived in the UK for 12 months after being given ILR can apply for British citizenship, if they also meet other requirements .
Under the government's plans, the standard length of time migrants will have to live in the UK to qualify for permanent settlement will double from five to 10 years.
Under this 10-year pathway, applicants must have earned at least £12,571 for five of the seven years immediately before being granted settlement.
However, there will be a shorter qualifying period of five years for certain groups, including:
People earning over £125,141 a year, as well as "highly skilled" migrants such as those on Global Talent or Innovator Founder visas, will qualify after three years.
Migrants who have claimed certain benefits or breached immigration rules will only be able to settle after at least 20 years.
To qualify for settlement, migrants will also have to meet other conditions including:
There will be a different set of rules for refugees – people who have been granted asylum in the UK because they are unable to return to their own country as they fear persecution.
Refugees who arrived in the UK through an official government scheme will qualify for settlement after five years.
However, other refugees will need to wait 10 years and either work or study.
Those who do not work or study will need to wait 20 years.
Refugees who arrived in the UK by small boat or another illegal route will have to wait 20 years if they work or study, and 30 years if they don't.
The changes will apply to migrants who are already in the UK but not those who have already been granted settlement.
A partner who arrives with someone who then applies for ILR will be able to settle at the same time, as long as they meet the relevant requirements.
However, a partner who joins later will need to complete the same qualifying residence period before they are eligible for settlement.
Eligible couples will be able to combine their earnings to meet the minimum income  requirement.
The household income threshold will be £25,142 – twice the individual minimum income requirement.
Children under 18 will continue to be able to settle with their parents.
They will be exempt from the income, government debt, English language and Life in the UK test requirements, but will remain subject to the relevant suitability and criminality requirements.
Young adults aged 18 to 24, who remain dependant on their family, will also continue to be able to settle alongside them.
They will be expected to meet all the adult mandatory requirements but not the individual income requirement.
Someone who is aged 25 or over when their family becomes eligible for settlement will be expected to qualify independently.
Eligible partners, parents and children of British citizens will continue to qualify for settlement after five years.

articles.title_orig: China Tech Stocks Get Fresh Lifeline From Beijing
articles.title_zh: China Tech Stocks Get Fresh Lifeline From Beijing
articles.content_orig:
Alibaba BABA , JD.com JD and PDD Holdings PDD moved higher in U.S. premarket trading Monday after Chinese regulators signaled a fresh effort to stabilize the country's battered stock market.
The move follows an 8.5% October drop in the CSI 300 , its worst monthly performance since early 2016. The benchmark had also fallen for 12 consecutive weeks, according to TipRanks.
Beijing is now stepping in with more liquidity.
The People's Bank of China said it will conduct a new swap operation Tuesday that could inject more than 100 billion yuan, or roughly $15 billion , into the equity market. Thirty-one brokerages and fund companies have already applied for quotas worth more than 100 billion yuan.
The swap facility allows securities firms, insurers and fund managers to exchange eligible assets for more liquid central-bank assets, giving them additional capacity to buy stocks.
China is also making its relending program for share repurchases and stake increases a long-term mechanism , while cutting the program's interest rate to 1% from 1.25% .
Regulators are applying pressure directly as well.
The China Securities Regulatory Commission urged major index constituents and leading technology companies to actively buy back shares , while also encouraging newer ETFs and fund managers to increase equity exposure during the downturn. Officials are separately studying whether to ease margin rules to improve market liquidity.
The policy response helped lift sentiment Monday, with the Shanghai Composite gaining 1.1% and the CSI 300 also moving higher.
Alibaba, JD and PDD have been caught in the broader decline as investors grapple with weak Chinese consumption, persistent property-sector problems and pressure across technology shares.
I think the key point here is that Beijing is sending a clearer message that it does not want the equity selloff to spiral.
For Alibaba, JD and PDD, that matters because their stocks have increasingly been trading on macro sentiment and policy risk, not just company fundamentals.
The latest measures can improve liquidity and potentially put a floor under sentiment.
But they do not fix the underlying issues by themselves.
China still needs stronger consumption, better economic momentum and more confidence in corporate earnings for the rally to become durable.
For investors, the key things to watch are how much of the new liquidity is actually deployed, whether corporate buybacks accelerate, and whether China follows these market-support steps with broader fiscal or economic stimulus .
The immediate signal is supportive.
The harder question is whether Beijing can turn that support into a lasting recovery.

articles.title_orig: Xbox’s former COO has ‘serious concerns’ about her abrupt departure
articles.title_zh: Xbox’s former COO has ‘serious concerns’ about her abrupt departure
articles.content_orig:
Helen Chiang is setting the record straight on her sudden exit from Microsoft.
Helen Chiang is setting the record straight on her sudden exit from Microsoft.
Xbox’s former chief operating officer, Helen Chiang, suddenly left Microsoft less than two weeks ago after being promoted into the role in July. I wrote in my Notepad newsletter last week that it seemed very weird for Chiang to suddenly depart Microsoft after 21 years with a surprisingly short memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. Now, Chiang says she has “serious concerns” about how she was treated.
In a lengthy LinkedIn post — entitled “clarity is kindness,” a reference to Sharma’s WSJ profile — Chiang doesn’t dispute that she was fired, but she doesn’t say why she was let go. Eurogamer reported last month that Chiang had been “terminated for policy violations,” but she says this is “not accurate.”
Chiang denies unfounded rumors that speculated she was leaking confidential information, or that she left to join a competitor. It’s clear the decision to leave Xbox was out of her hands. “You don’t spend two decades somewhere without developing a deep loyalty to the people, teams, and businesses you’ve helped build,” says Chiang. “Xbox was never just another stop in my career. My end game was always to keep building here.”
She also denies engaging in “discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity.” Like I wrote in Notepad last week , Chiang has been described to me by multiple Xbox employees as highly respected, with high integrity. “I stand by my record: both the results I delivered and the way I have treated people throughout my career,” says Chiang.
The most significant part of Chiang’s post is a paragraph on fairness and accountability, hinting that she wasn’t treated fairly:
I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently. I have serious concerns about how they were applied in my case, and I believe those concerns deserve to be taken seriously.
Chiang also says “This is not how I ever imagined my story here would end. And it is not the whole story.”
We’ve reached out to Chiang to ask if she’s pursuing legal action against Microsoft. We’ve also asked Microsoft to comment on Chiang’s post, but the company didn’t respond in time for publication.

articles.title_orig: US petrol prices dip ahead of midterms as voters eye costs
articles.title_zh: US petrol prices dip ahead of midterms as voters eye costs
articles.content_orig:
Petrol prices have dipped amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran, but remain high ahead of the United States midterm elections , as the cost of living remains a central issue for voters.
On Monday, the average price for a gallon (3.78 litres) of regular petrol was $4.17, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. That is down 12 cents from this time last week and 23 cents from a month ago.
By comparison, prices were $3.04 this time a year ago and $2.98 on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.
Diesel fuel prices remain high at $6.29 per gallon, but that is down 6 cents from this time last week. Diesel prices climbed above $6 a gallon for the first time in September before topping out at $6.53.
The average petrol price of President Donald Trump’s second term to date was set to exceed $3.46 a gallon on Monday, surpassing the previous record for a presidential administration set under former President Joe Biden, according to a Financial Times analysis of federal data.
Oil prices are continuing to fall, down 6 percent on Monday as diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran continued following in-person talks in Qatar over the weekend.
“Oil markets down significantly this morning after Trump signalled he favoured negotiations and not new attacks on Iran,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X. “Oil down [approximately] 5%, wholesale gasoline and diesel pointing to roughly 16 [cents per gallon] decline. The national average could fall under $4 a gallon in the next week barring a course change.”
Cost-of-living issues remain top of mind for US voters as they head to the polls. An Associated Press-NORC poll last month found that a majority of Americans believe addressing cost-of-living issues should be a priority for Congress, including 78 percent of Republicans and 89 percent of Democrats.
“Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Al Jazeera. “Protecting America’s national security from threats by a radical terrorist regime that has chanted ‘Death to America’ for 47 years was the right thing to do – and President Trump is the only president who has had the courage to do it.”
Rogers added, “Thanks to the exceptional work of the US military, more oil is now flowing out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran conflict began.”
On Wall Street, oil and gas giant stocks were trending downward in midday trading. ConocoPhillips was down 3.7 percent, Chevron 2.3 percent and ExxonMobil 3.3 percent.
The major US indices more broadly were in positive territory. The Nasdaq was up 0.7 percent, the S&P 500 0.6 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average 1 percent.

articles.title_orig: Marvell doubles down on AI boom with costly $115 billion Lumentum deal
articles.title_zh: Marvell doubles down on AI boom with costly $115 billion Lumentum deal
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology 's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday.
"You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here."
Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.
Marvell shares slumped 8% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank 13%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch.
Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models.
"We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said.
Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.
Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.
This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.
Marvell 's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies.
In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers.
"This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them."
Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.
CORRECTION: This story has been updated to reflect that Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston described the deal as an 'enormous' opportunity. A previous version of this story incorrectly cited the Marvell CEO.

articles.title_orig: How China Might Target US Midterms - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.title_zh: How China Might Target US Midterms - Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA)
articles.content_orig:
No research shows Chinese propaganda or disinformation playing a pivotal role in the midterm elections, particularly when compared to Russia’s aggressive attempts. Yet significant blind spots exist. If it desired, Beijing is well-positioned to shape political debate through the WeChat app and through Chinese AI models.
Rather than shifting control of Congress, Beijing’s goal would likely be to reduce the presence of known Communist Party critics, particularly those serving in the Congressional-Executive Commission on China. Created by Congress in October 2000, the Commission monitors Chinese human rights and rule of law.
Several competitive races feature Commission members, including former Senator Sherrod Brown in Ohio and current Commission Chair Dan Sullivan in Alaska. House races in Iowa and Virginia involve current Commission members Zach Nunn and Jen Kiggans. Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate in Iowa, is on the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, another Congressional body critical of the regime.
Texas looks particularly sensitive for a different reason. WeChat , a messaging and multi-function app, has an estimated 1.5 million US users, concentrated in states with large Chinese American populations. Chinese Americans make up roughly one percent of Texas’s population .
Chinese state-sponsored censorship on WeChat is well-documented. A 2025 University of Texas study based on interviews with 20 Chinese Americans in Texas detailed how political misinformation circulates on the platform. One young interviewee described how her father read that an Asian American woman had been elected mayor of Boston months before the actual election.
“He just accepts everything he reads, and then he just forwards it,” she said. “My mother-in-law, too.”
Cultural and social pressures reduce willingness to correct misinformation in family or friend groups. “It doesn’t feel right for me to talk bad to my elders, especially in the group chat setting,” a 19-year-old Chinese American explained.
In this environment, the app is powerful. “A lot of people don’t know who to vote for, so they are easily swayed,” another interviewee commented. “It is a big political platform, and a lot of people will just blindly follow.”
The 2026 elections are the first to take place in an environment where AI chatbots are widely available. About one-fifth of Americans plan to use AI tools to help learn about candidates or inform voting decisions, according to a recent survey . Most will turn to American models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Perplexity, but many US developers are increasingly relying on Chinese-origin models such as DeepSeek and Qwen, allowing them to enter the US information environment.
These models reflect the Chinese government’s official stances on domestic politics and human rights. Censorship and propaganda have also been found in responses to questions about US press freedom and elections.
One study examined Chinese AI models’ responses to questions about the upcoming US elections. Conducted by a research group based in Europe, researchers tested seven AI models (five US and two Chinese) with a set of 20 polling-style questions.
All models proved relatively consistent and offered mixed results in terms of partisan preferences. The two Chinese models did not diverge sharply from their US counterparts in their responses. DeepSeek, for example, selected the Democratic option on two questions about which party’s candidate it would select for Congress and which party it prefers to control Congress. So did Claude and Perplexity (99% on one of the questions). By contrast, Qwen chose Democrats 55% and 75% of the time, respectively.
The results are striking for what they show about the leeway allowed the Chinese models to comment on US versus Chinese politics. DeepSeek offered critical assessments of the US president’s job performance. Asking the same questions about Chinese President Xi Jinping would almost certainly produce refusals or strictly glowing reviews.
Major holes remain in our understanding of where and how Chinese Communist Party-linked electoral influence could be occurring. Researchers, election monitors, and others focused on election integrity should address these gaps — particularly before the 2028 elections.
Sarah Cook is founder of China Rights Analytics and Advising LLC and author of the UnderReported China newsletter.

articles.title_orig: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights
articles.title_zh: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.
People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display . The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.
The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.
However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households. Is there a market for a smart home device costing more than $1,000 that moves around while hosting FaceTime calls, automatically handling room lights, and occasionally ordering the family cat to get off the dining table?
One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years. The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.
Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information. The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI .
From a technical and safety standpoint, Apple’s initial focus on a limited-purpose home robot still makes much more sense right now than any attempt to develop a general-purpose autonomous robot that could pose greater risks when operating near humans . The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu and Eisenkot Seek Shot to Be Israel’s Premier
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu and Eisenkot Seek Shot to Be Israel’s Premier
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has lost his coalition’s parliamentary majority following legislative elections on October 27.
But a bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu also failed to win a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, leaving Israel without a clear path to a new government.
What’s ahead is likely weeks of political wrangling as Israel’s disparate factions weigh possible governing arrangements, including a unity government bringing rival factions together or a minority government reliant on outside support. If they fail to reach an agreement, Israel could head back to the polls.
Here’s what you should know:
The pro-Netanyahu coalition won 53 seats:
A bloc of Jewish parties opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats:
Arab-led parties won 19 seats:
That leaves all existing blocs short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, meaning some parties would have to realign or join forces across bloc lines to form a new government.
Israel’s election results must be officially certified and presented to President Isaac Herzog by November 4 .
The new Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on November 10 .
Herzog must task one incoming Knesset member with forming a new government by November 11 . He is expected to make his decision with input from party leaders, selecting the candidate he believes has the best chance of building a coalition.
The candidate commissioned by Herzog has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible extension of 14 days .
He has not said yet, but the most likely candidates are Netanyahu or former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar party received the most votes in the opposition bloc.
According to Israel’s Yedioth Ahronoth media, Eisenkot may have an edge over Netanyahu as some Arab-led parties consider endorsing him in a bid to oust Netanyahu.
Herzog, for his part, has urged Israeli politicians to move away from rigid partisan stances and look for “creative solutions” that will lead to a new government and avoid a second round of elections.
Before the election, Herzog said he would do everything he could to spare the country another election cycle, even if that means pressing for a national unity government that brings together rivals Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have previously ruled out partnering with the Arab-led parties .
Former Prime Minister Ehud Barak, however, has said he believes they “can change their mind”, arguing that Netanyahu would do in their position.
“If Netanyahu had a similar problem, he would immediately invite Mansour Abbas”, the leader of Ra’am and “give him the role of a minister of interior”, Barak told France 24 on Friday.
Abbas himself has signalled a willingness to work the opposition camp, saying Eisenkot’s conditions would not pose an obstacle for his party, according to Israel’s Channel 12.
Yousef Jabareen from the Arab-led Joint List has also said that his party is ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”.
“The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote on X.
Even if Arab-led parties do not formally join the opposition’s coalition, they could prop it up from outside by helping it pass a confidence vote in the Knesset.
Raluca Ganea, co-founder of Israeli civil society group Zazim, told Al Jazeera that a coalition between the opposition bloc and the Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel “is the only path forward for Israeli democracy as a whole”.
If Herzog’s first candidate fails to form a government within the 42 days, the Israeli president has the option of asking another Knesset member to try to do so within 28 days. If that candidate also fails, a majority of Knesset members could put forward a third candidate, who would have a final 14 days to try to assemble one.
Even without a coalition commanding at least 61 seats, a candidate could still try to form a minority government by relying on outside support from smaller parties, including Arab-led parties, or negotiate a power-sharing arrangement with alternating prime ministers.
If none of these options succeed and deadlock persists, the Knesset would be formally dissolved, and Israelis would return to the polls for another round of elections.
Those elections would have to be called within 90 days.
Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed.
If the process drags out, that could leave Israel’s longest-serving prime minister in power for months more, even if he ultimately fails to become part of the next governing coalition.

articles.title_orig: Chili’s customers in North Carolina suffer burns after sipping margaritas mistakenly made with cleaning chemical
articles.title_zh: Chili’s customers in North Carolina suffer burns after sipping margaritas mistakenly made with cleaning chemical
articles.content_orig:
A Chili’s Grill & Bar in North Carolina is back in business after three customers and two workers suffered chemical burns on their mouths from sipping margaritas mistakenly made with a cleaning chemical last week.
The eatery in Forest City was shut down on Thursday after the customers, who had ordered the drinks shortly after the restaurant opened for lunch, “immediately experienced discomfort and chemical burns in and around their mouths,” the Foothills Health District said in a statement.
“Two restaurant employees subsequently tasted the substance and reported similar symptoms,” the FHD statement.
It was reopened the next day after local health inspectors discovered that a worker “preparing the bar for lunch service discovered the unlabeled container and, believing its contents to be sugar, used the chemical to prepare the margarita station.”
Chili’s, according to its menu , offers several margaritas that are make with a “citrus-sugar rimmer” in addition to the traditional salt.
FHD spokesperson Megan Rollins said in an email the investigation was closed and no fines were issued. She said the injured parties received medical treatment, but had no information about their conditions.
A Chili’s spokesperson said in an email that this was an “incident isolated to a single restaurant in Forest City, North Carolina, that resulted in injuries to two of our guests and Team Members.”
“Our team took immediate action to support those affected and avoid further injuries,” the spokesperson said. “We have thoroughly investigated the circumstances and addressed the issues specific to this location.”
The spokesperson did not respond to a follow-up question from NBC News seeking an explanation for why their tally of injured customers was different from the one provided earlier by the FHD.
This Chili’s is located about 60 miles west of Charlotte, North Carolina.
On the morning of Oct. 26, according to the FHD statement, “a restaurant employee received a granulated degreasing chemical from a contracted worker who was power washing the exterior, and placed it into an unlabeled container.”
For reasons unclear, “the container was brought inside the restaurant and left in the bar area.”
Two days later, those chemicals were inadvertently added to margaritas.
Corky Siemaszko is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: China Is Sending AI-Powered Robots Into the Ocean to Uncover Its Lost Ancient History
articles.title_zh: China Is Sending AI-Powered Robots Into the Ocean to Uncover Its Lost Ancient History
articles.content_orig:
China's next five-year archaeological plan, covering 2026 to 2030 , proposes deploying artificial intelligence, ancient-DNA analysis, remote sensing and deep-sea robots across some of the country's most significant historical sites. The program is designed to recover artifacts, reconstruct damaged objects and investigate questions about human migration, early states and maritime trade that conventional excavation has so far left only partially answered.
Excavations routinely produce large quantities of broken, scattered material whose connections are difficult to establish manually. Specialized AI systems would identify artifact fragments, match pieces to one another and generate virtual restorations , allowing researchers to study an object's probable original appearance without physically altering the surviving material.
Each pillar of the plan addresses a distinct limitation of conventional archaeological methods.
Remote sensing , which uses aerial or satellite data to detect buried structures, could help researchers locate remains before excavation begins. Ancient-DNA analysis would contribute to population research, tracing relationships, migrations and environmental adaptation among communities that lived thousands of years ago. Usable results require biological material preserved well enough to avoid contamination.
Underwater robotics addresses sites that human divers cannot safely reach. The plan calls for purpose-built deep-sea robots , specialized diving equipment and precision excavation tools aimed at shipwrecks and Maritime Silk Road routes lying on the seabed.
Institutionally, the program is intended to be permanent rather than a series of isolated projects. The official plan describes a national-level archaeological laboratory and a maritime-archaeology hub in Qingdao, signaling an effort to embed high-technology research into standing infrastructure.
Named sites and international partnerships give the blueprint a concrete geographic scope.
Research targets extend from northern China's earliest known sites through the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau and across Eurasia. Among the domestic priorities is the transition from Paleolithic hunter-gatherer life to agriculture and settled communities along the Yellow River, Yangtze River and southern Lingnan region.
Major Bronze Age and early-state sites, including Sanxingdui , Erlitou and Yinxu, feature prominently alongside historical infrastructure such as the Qin dynasty Direct Road, the Great Wall and the Grand Canal. International partnerships with institutions in Egypt, Greece, Saudi Arabia and Tunisia are planned for comparative research, underwater surveys and heritage preservation.
The Nanhai No. 1 shows what underwater excavation can recover and what it demands in return.
The Nanhai No. 1 , a Southern Song-era merchant vessel associated with trade between China and overseas markets, illustrates why underwater archaeology occupies a central place in the new blueprint. Discovered in 1987 and raised intact in 2007, the wreck was transferred to a purpose-built aquatic environment at the Guangdong Maritime Silk Road Museum, where conservation and excavation continue under controlled conditions.
UNESCO describes the site as unusually valuable because its preservation captures cargo and food remains that document commerce and daily life aboard the vessel. According to a government-linked report, more than 180,000 cultural relics have been salvaged and preserved from the site.
Ambition and evidence are not the same thing, and the plan's limits deserve equal billing.
AI cannot reconstruct information the surviving evidence does not support; a virtual restoration is only as reliable as the fragments behind it. Deep-sea robots still contend with pressure, poor visibility, currents and fragile materials.
Ancient-DNA results depend on preservation conditions and rigorous contamination controls, and their interpretation requires care. None of this invalidates the program's potential, but discovery and conclusion are not the same thing.
The blueprint's stated cultural objectives are as significant as its scientific ones, and they invite scrutiny.
The plan carries an explicit cultural objective alongside its scientific aims: increasing China's international influence over interpretations of its history and civilization. That goal raises practical questions about data access, interpretive independence and the terms under which foreign institutions will participate. How those questions are answered will determine whether the international partnerships function as genuine scholarly collaboration or primarily serve a national framing agenda. Those details remain unclear and will merit close attention as the program moves from blueprint to fieldwork.

articles.content_orig:

Microsoft's COO Helen Chiang was fired from Xbox a few weeks ago, after 27 years of top-level leadership spent across the org, most prolifically at Minecraft.
The removal was abrupt and somewhat confusing on the face of it. Chiang was widely respected across the Microsoft stack and is a trusted figure, described to me as "by the book" by our own sources. When it emerged that she had been fired for "policy violations," it added an unexpected twist that left us with more questions than answers, ultimately.
Now, Helen Chiang has responded to the incident on LinkedIn , titled "Clarity is Kindness," which is a comment Xbox CEO Asha Sharma made to the WSJ while discussing the health of Microsoft's gaming business recently.
There has been some speculation about my abrupt departure from Microsoft, including claims that I was “fired for a policy violation”. That’s not accurate," Chiang writes, "silence should not be mistaken for agreement. What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize. It’s important to me to set the record straight."
In the full post shared below, Chiang denies that she leaked information, sought employment at Microsoft competitors, engaged in insider trading, bullying, or embezzlement, or that she left because she didn't get the CEO job. She says that she always hoped to stay at Microsoft and "keep building," and this departure wasn't what she envisioned.
" I share this because I don’t want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal."
As to not paraphrase, I've included the full text from the post below.
There has been some speculation about my abrupt departure from Microsoft, including claims that I was “fired for a policy violation”. That’s not accurate and while I won’t turn this into a play-by-play, silence should not be mistaken for agreement. What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize. It’s important to me to set the record straight. First, I did not leak confidential company information to the press. I have never communicated with any journalist outside the limited, company-authorized interviews I’ve done as part of my job. That includes every journalist who reached out this week seeking my side of the story. Second, I did not leave XBOX to join a competitor. You don’t spend two decades somewhere without developing a deep loyalty to the people, teams, and businesses you’ve helped build. XBOX was never just another stop in my career. My end game was always to keep building here. Third, I did not engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity. I stand by my record: both the results I delivered and the way I have treated people throughout my career. I won’t let speculation define my character or erase that record. Lastly, I did not leave because I was passed over for a bigger role. Since having children, I’ve been intentional about how I define ambition and success. I haven’t actively sought out bigger roles or increased responsibilities, and the last time I interviewed for a job was in 2011. My reputation and results paved the way for the opportunities that followed. I went where the company believed I was needed and where I could have the greatest impact. I did not ask for my most recent role, either. I was promoted into it in July. I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others. Those standards only mean something when they’re applied consistently. I have serious concerns about how they were applied in my case, and I believe those concerns deserve to be taken seriously. I share this because I don’t want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind. To everyone who has reached out with hugs, love, and support: thank you. So many of you have reminded me of the wonderful times we’ve shared over the past 20 years and the impact we’ve had on one another. Some of you I haven’t been in touch with for several years, yet you still took the time to check on me. Others are people I’ve never even met, but you reached out anyway. That speaks volumes about the care and humanity in our industry and the connections that transcend where we work. This is not how I ever imagined my story here would end. And it is not the whole story." — Helen Chiang, former Xbox COO.
Helen Chiang's somewhat unceremonious departure comes amidst widespread upheaval at Xbox as Microsoft restructures its gaming org , which has led to thousands of layoffs, divestitures, and studio closures. Microsoft managed to return some studios to independent ownership and has sold others to publishers, as it tries to rein in spending in general.
The Coalition has been put on the hook for $500 million per Microsoft's finance auditors, who only see the dollars and not the complexity of game development, the impact the pandemic had on the development of games between Gears 5 and E-Day, and other mitigating factors.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has returned the brand's focus to its core customers in recent months, with a return of exclusive games, boosting investment in the existing console infrastructure, and improving things on the back end for game developers.
I suspect there'll be more disruption before things calm down ... as the industry in general reels from an overabundance of content, reduced consumer spending, and the AI -fostered RAMpocalypse .

Jez is known for breaking exclusive news and analysis as relates to the Microsoft ecosystem — while being powered by tea.
